Fresh food is displayed at a market.
Pexels · 18312070
Choosing with care
A good way to buy what we need combines practical structure with an awareness of other people. Neither a rigid plan nor complete
improvisation is sufficient on its own; both need to be judged in context.
The practical case is straightforward: a short shopping list helps us buy only what we can use. Consider how we check the kitchen before
choosing fruit and vegetables. The benefit is not merely efficiency. A modest arrangement prevents avoidable confusion, leaving attention
available for the activity itself rather than for problems that could have been anticipated.
Consideration adds a second, equally important dimension: asking questions helps us compare choices fairly. In this situation, we ask how
long the bread will keep before deciding how much to buy. A decision can be convenient for one person while creating difficulty for another, so
its value depends partly on whose needs it recognises.
The most useful approach therefore brings structure and consideration together. Preparation establishes a workable starting point; attention to
other people keeps it responsive. Success should be assessed by how well the arrangement serves the experience, rather than by how
closely events follow the original plan.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion. Each body
paragraph needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.
Discuss the claim that more preparation always helps people buy what we need. Support a qualified position with two concrete examples.
Use four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion. (Model: One possible outline: introduce the situation; discuss a
short shopping list helps us buy only what we can use with an example; discuss asking questions helps us compare choices fairly with a
different example; conclude by connecting the two points.)
